# avrdude

**Reads and writes AVR microcontroller memories through almost any programmer**

- **Version recorded:** 7.1
- **Categories:** `programmer`
- **Upstream:** <https://github.com/avrdudes/avrdude>

## What it does

Uploads, downloads and verifies the flash, EEPROM and fuse bytes of an AVR — the ATmega and ATtiny families, and the AVR core inside most classic Arduino boards — through a very long list of programmers.

## Why you would want it

It is what the Arduino IDE shells out to, so knowing it directly means being able to flash a board without the IDE, script a production run, or recover a chip whose fuses were set wrong. It also reaches programmers no IDE offers.

## Before it will work

A programmer, and for the older ones a serial or parallel port. Access for the USB ones comes from the `programmer` hardware class.

## Install and launch

- **Installed with the profile:** [`electronics`](../profiles/electronics.md).
- **Install:** `hammunition install avrdude --dry-run`, read the plan, then run it without `--dry-run`.
- **Launch:** Its package ships its own commands and application-menu entry; a unit that ships none gets a generated terminal entry (**D-050**). `hammunition status` lists what is installed.
- **The install needs the network to:** your distribution's package archive.

## Offline use

*Not yet documented for this application.* Read “Before it will work” above for what it needs; the install-time network line above is the only offline fact generated from the manifest. Internet, a local network and a radio link are three different things, and this page does not claim any of them works until it says so.

## How it installs

- apt: `avrdude`

## Known problems

Setting fuse bytes wrongly can make a chip unreachable by the programmer that set them — a low-voltage-programming or clock-source fuse can require a high-voltage programmer to recover. This is not a bug and it is the most common way an AVR ends up in a drawer.

    Its identifiers (counted by the generated programmer class, not
    here) include `16c0:05dc`, the USBasp, which is one of
Objective Development's shared V-USB pairs and not an identifier for any product. `libhamlib4t64` claims it too.
